title: RDP Logon From New ASN
summary: RDP logon from a new autonomous system number detection flags successful interactive remote desktop sessions where the source network has never previously appeared in the organisation's remote access history for that host, account or user population. The behaviour matters because stolen credentials are frequently valid, correctly typed and correctly MFA-challenged, so the only observable difference between a legitimate administrator and an intruder is often where the session originates and whether the ASN, country or hosting provider is consistent with that account's history. The telemetry required is authentication logging from the remote access path itself, including source address, account, session outcome and negotiated protocol, combined with an enrichment source that maps addresses to autonomous system numbers and network ownership, plus asset inventory so the target host's business function is known. The signal survives common evasion because residential proxy services and commercial hosting providers are themselves registries with stable ASN values, so an operator routing through a bulletproof host or a cloud virtual machine still produces a source that stands out against an enterprise user base; even a compromised home router in a previously unseen ASN deviates from the account baseline. The detection breaks down in practice for a well known set of reasons: travelling staff, remote work relocations, mobile carrier address pools that rotate ASN frequently, and legitimate use of VPN egress concentrators all generate genuine first-seen ASNs. It also fails when enrichment data is stale or when the source address seen by the collector is a load balancer or gateway rather than the true client, which is common where a reverse proxy terminates the session. Effective use therefore depends on scoring first-seen ASN alongside impossible travel, account privilege, MFA method used, and post-authentication behaviour rather than alerting on first-seen alone.
objectives: Explain why source network reputation and ASN history remain useful when credentials and MFA are both valid.
Build a query that joins successful remote desktop authentication to an ASN enrichment table and computes first-seen combinations.
Score alerts using account privilege, host business function, hosting-origin flag and MFA method rather than geography alone.
Identify telemetry blind spots created by reverse proxies, jump hosts and VPN concentrators that obscure the true client address.
Distinguish a compromised but valid session from credential misuse by examining post-authentication actions on the target host.
Document an investigation timeline for a suspected remote access intrusion suitable for a formal incident report.
dataSources: Windows Security event 4624 logon records with logon type 10 for remote interactive sessions, including source address
Remote desktop gateway or jump host operational logs recording client address, account and session duration
Identity provider sign-in logs containing source address, applied conditional access policy and authentication method
Address-to-ASN and network ownership enrichment table refreshed from a commercial or public routing registry
Asset inventory mapping host names to business function, environment and data classification
logic: Take every successful remote interactive authentication, resolve the source address to an autonomous system and country, and compare the combination against the historical set of ASNs seen for that account, that host and the tenant as a whole. Raise an alert when the source ASN is new for the account or host, and add weight when the origin belongs to a hosting or proxy provider, when the account holds administrative rights, when the target is a server rather than a workstation, or when the sign-in used a weaker authentication method than the account normally uses. Correlate the session with actions taken on the target host afterwards so that a genuinely suspicious remote session can be distinguished from a travelling employee connecting from a hotel network.
pseudoQuery:
title: Remote Desktop Logon From Previously Unseen ASN
id: det-rdp-new-asn
status: training
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  successful_rdp:
    EventID: 4624
    LogonType: 10
    # status field indicates success
  source_enriched:
    SourceAsn|exists: true
  first_seen_asn:
    condition: source_enriched and asn_not_in_historical_baseline(AccountName, SourceAsn, 90d)
  risky_origin:
    AsnCategory:
      - hosting
      - proxy
      - anonymiser
  privileged_account:
    AccountName|endswith:
      - '-adm'
      - '-da'
  condition: successful_rdp and first_seen_asn and (risky_origin or privileged_account)
fields:
  - AccountName
  - SourceIpAddress
  - SourceAsn
  - TargetHostName
  - AuthenticationMethod
level: high
falsePositives: Employees travelling or relocating who connect from a genuinely new network provider
Mobile broadband and carrier grade NAT pools that present different ASNs across sessions
Vendors and contractors connecting from their own corporate ranges for the first time
Cloud hosted jump hosts or administrative workstations provisioned in a new region
Users on dynamic residential connections whose ISP reassigns address blocks between providers
tuningNotes: Set the historical baseline window long enough to cover seasonal working patterns, commonly ninety days or more, and compute it per account and per host rather than only per tenant so a new workstation does not immediately generate alerts for every user. Treat hosting and anonymising ASN categories as a separate higher severity rule rather than folding them into the base rule, which keeps the general detection useful without paging on every business trip. Feed known corporate egress ranges, VPN concentrators and vendor ranges into an explicit allow-list and revisit it monthly, and normalise the source address at the collector so that reverse proxies and gateways do not mask the true client. Finally, cap the number of alerts per account per day so that a single user on a rotating mobile connection cannot flood the queue.

beginner.definition: Remote Desktop lets you control another computer over the network, and each connection comes from an internet address. An autonomous system number is a label for the network that owns that address. This detection flags a successful remote desktop login from a network that is new for that account or that computer.
beginner.whyItMatters: Stolen passwords are often typed correctly, so a login can look perfectly normal. Multi-factor authentication may even pass if the attacker holds the code. The strongest remaining clue is where the session comes from. An account may always connect from one city, then suddenly arrive from an unknown provider abroad. That change deserves a look before the intruder moves deeper.
howItWorks: Your systems log every successful remote desktop login, including the source address and the account used.
An enrichment step turns each address into the network provider that owns it and the country it sits in.
You store the usual networks for each account and each computer over the past weeks or months.
A comparison step checks whether the network behind a new login has ever appeared before.
The alert ranks higher when the network is a hosting or proxy provider, not a home internet line.
Analysts then confirm whether the account holder was travelling or whether the session came from a stranger.
beginner.example: Think of an office where everyone badges in at the front door. Security knows which door each person normally uses. One morning a badge appears at a service entrance on the far side of the building. That person has never touched that door before. The badge is real and the door is real, yet the guard should still walk over and look. A first-time network is a reason to check, not proof of guilt.
takeaways: When passwords and codes can be stolen, where a session starts is a useful clue.
A new source network is a signal to investigate, not a verdict.
Many new networks at once usually means your records moved, not your users.
